title: Linux and macOS support basics
summary: Get comfortable supporting the two non-Windows systems you will meet: navigate and manage a Linux box from the terminal, and handle common macOS tasks for Apple users.
objectives: Navigate a Linux filesystem and inspect files from the terminal
Use sudo and chmod to manage permissions safely
Install and update software with a package manager like apt
Check disk, memory and processes with df, top and ps
Perform common macOS support tasks and manage software with Homebrew
Know where logs and settings live on Linux and macOS

quiz.q: Which command changes the permissions on a file in Linux?
quiz.why: chmod (change mode) sets the read, write and execute permissions on a file or directory; the others change directory, check a Windows disk, or are not real commands.

quiz.q: What does prefixing a command with sudo do?
options: Runs it as the superuser (root) for that command
quiz.why: sudo (superuser do) runs a single command with administrative/root privileges, which is the safe way to perform admin tasks without logging in as root.

quiz.q: On a Debian/Ubuntu system, which command installs a package and its dependencies?
quiz.why: On Debian and Ubuntu the apt package manager handles installs; sudo apt install <package> downloads and installs the package with its dependencies.

quiz.q: A Mac user's application won't quit normally. What is the standard macOS way to force it to close?
options: Force Quit (Cmd+Option+Esc) or kill from Activity Monitor
quiz.why: macOS uses Force Quit, reached with Command-Option-Escape or from Activity Monitor, to close an unresponsive app — there is no Ctrl+Alt+Delete on a Mac.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain what df and top tell you on a Linux machine.
quiz.answer: df shows how much disk space is used and free on each filesystem, while top shows the running processes with their live CPU and memory usage.
quiz.why: df is for storage capacity and top is for live performance and what's consuming CPU/RAM — two of the first things you check when a Linux box is slow or full.

quiz.q: Where would you look first to investigate a problem on a Linux server?
quiz.answer: In the system and application logs, typically under /var/log (for example /var/log/syslog or with the journalctl command on systemd systems).
quiz.why: Linux records events and errors in /var/log and the systemd journal, so that's the first place a technician checks to see what actually went wrong.

body_markdown:
## Why you need more than Windows

Not every machine on the helpdesk runs Windows. Developers, designers and servers run **Linux** and **macOS**, and a confident technician can support all three. The good news: both Linux and macOS share a **Unix** heritage, so the terminal skills you learn here work on both. Once you are comfortable at a shell, a strange-looking system stops being intimidating.

## Moving around Linux

Everything in Linux is a file, and you navigate from the terminal. The essentials:

```bash
pwd            # print working directory
ls -la         # list everything, long format, including hidden files
cd /var/log    # change directory
cat syslog     # show a file's contents
```

Sample output:

```bash
$ ls -la
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 Jun 16 09:01 .
-rw-r--r--  1 user user  220 Jun 16 08:55 notes.txt
```

That `drwxr-xr-x` string is the **permissions** — read, write, execute for the owner, group and everyone else.

## Permissions, sudo and packages

To change permissions you use **chmod**; to act as the administrator (**root**) for one command you prefix it with **sudo**. To install software on Debian/Ubuntu you use the **apt** package manager.

```bash
chmod +x script.sh           # make a script executable
sudo apt update              # refresh the package list
sudo apt install htop        # install a package and its dependencies
```

Using `sudo` for single commands — rather than logging in as root — is the safe Linux equivalent of least privilege.

## Checking health: disk, memory, processes

When a Linux box is slow or full, three commands answer most questions:

```bash
df -h          # disk space used/free, human-readable
top            # live processes by CPU/memory (press q to quit)
ps aux         # snapshot of all running processes
```

Sample output:

```bash
$ df -h
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        50G   42G  5.2G  90% /
```

Ninety percent full explains a lot. For deeper investigation, logs live in **/var/log** (or via `journalctl` on modern systems).

## Supporting macOS

macOS is Unix underneath, so the same terminal commands work in **Terminal.app**. Day to day you will also use the graphical tools: **Activity Monitor** (the Mac equivalent of Task Manager), **Force Quit** (Cmd+Option+Esc) for a frozen app, **Disk Utility** for drives, and **Time Machine** for backups. For installing developer tools, many Mac users rely on **Homebrew**:

```bash
brew update              # refresh Homebrew
brew install wget        # install a package
brew list                # what's installed
```

You can also read and change hidden settings with `defaults`:

```bash
defaults write com.apple.finder AppleShowAllFiles -bool true
killall Finder           # apply the change
```

## Your task

Get to a Linux shell (a VM, WSL on Windows, or a Raspberry Pi) and do the following: run `pwd`, `ls -la`, and `df -h`, and note your home directory and how full the disk is. Create a file, then use `chmod +x` to make it executable and confirm the permissions changed. Use `sudo apt update` (or your distro's package manager) to refresh the package list. If you have access to a Mac, open Activity Monitor, find the most CPU-hungry process, and write one sentence on what it is and whether it looks normal.

The good news is that both Linux and Mac share a Unix heritage, so the terminal skills you learn here work on both systems. slides.title: Moving around Linux
bullets: p-w-d prints your current directory.
l-s dash l-a lists everything, including hidden.
c-d changes directory.
cat shows a file's contents.
slides.narration: Everything in Linux is a file, and you navigate from the terminal. P-w-d prints your working directory, so you always know where you are. L-s dash l-a lists everything in long format, including hidden files. c-d changes directory; here we move into slash var slash log. And cat shows a file's contents. Those four commands get you moving around any Linux system.

slides.title: Reading permissions
bullets: The d-r-w-x string shows permissions.
Read, write, execute for owner, group, others.
A leading d means it's a directory.
Permissions control who can do what.
slides.code:
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 Jun 16 09:01 .
-rw-r--r--  1 user user  220 Jun 16 08:55 notes.txt
slides.narration: When you list files, you'll see a string like d-r-w-x-r-minus-x-r-minus-x at the start of each line. That's the permissions. It shows read, write, and execute rights for the owner, the group, and everyone else. A leading d means it's a directory; a dash means a regular file. Reading that string tells you instantly who's allowed to do what with each file.

slides.title: chmod, sudo and apt
bullets: chmod changes permissions.
sudo runs one command as root.
apt installs software on Debian and Ubuntu.
sudo for single commands = least privilege.
slides.code:
chmod +x script.sh
sudo apt update
sudo apt install htop
slides.narration: Three commands you'll use constantly. Ch-mod changes permissions; ch-mod plus x makes a script executable. Soo-doo runs a single command as the superuser, root, which is the safe way to do admin work without logging in as root. And on Debian or Ubuntu, apt is the package manager; soo-doo apt update refreshes the list, and soo-doo apt install fetches a package and its dependencies.

slides.title: Checking system health
bullets: d-f dash h shows disk space.
top shows live processes by CPU and memory.
p-s a-u-x is a snapshot of processes.
Press q to quit top.
slides.narration: When a Linux box is slow or full, three commands answer most questions. D-f dash h shows disk space used and free, in human-readable sizes. Top shows live processes ordered by C-P-U and memory; press q to quit it. And p-s a-u-x gives a one-time snapshot of every running process. If d-f dash h shows the disk ninety percent full, you've often found your problem already.

slides.title: Where Linux keeps logs
bullets: System logs live under /var/log.
For example /var/log/syslog.
Modern systems use journalctl.
Logs are your first stop for errors.
slides.narration: When something goes wrong on Linux, the logs are your first stop. They live under slash var slash log, for example slash var slash log slash syslog. On modern systems that use systemd, you read the journal with journal-c-t-l, often journal-c-t-l dash x-e to see recent errors. Before you guess at a fix, read the log; it usually tells you exactly what failed.

slides.title: Supporting macOS
bullets: macOS is Unix; the same commands work.
Activity Monitor = Task Manager.
Force Quit with Cmd-Option-Escape.
Time Machine handles backups.
slides.code:
brew update
brew install wget
brew list
slides.narration: macOS is Unix underneath, so the same terminal commands work in Terminal dot app. Day to day you'll also use the graphical tools: Activity Monitor is the Mac's Task Manager, Force Quit with Command-Option-Escape closes a frozen app, and Time Machine handles backups. For installing developer tools, many Mac users rely on Homebrew: brew update, brew install, and brew list manage software from the terminal.

slides.title: macOS settings with defaults
bullets: defaults reads and writes hidden settings.
Example: show all files in Finder.
killall restarts an app to apply changes.
Powerful, so change with care.
slides.code:
defaults write com.apple.finder AppleShowAllFiles -bool true
killall Finder
slides.narration: Macs also let you read and change hidden settings from the terminal with the defaults command. For example, defaults write com dot apple dot finder, apple-show-all-files, true, makes Finder show hidden files. Then kill-all Finder restarts Finder so the change takes effect. It's powerful, so change settings carefully and note what you changed in case you need to put it back.

bullets: Navigate Linux with pwd, ls, cd, cat.
Manage access with chmod and sudo.
Install with apt; check health with df, top, ps.
macOS: Activity Monitor, Force Quit, Homebrew.
Task: explore a Linux shell, inspect a Mac.
slides.narration: Let's recap. You navigate Linux with p-w-d, l-s, c-d, and cat. You manage access with ch-mod and soo-doo. You install software with apt, and check health with d-f, top, and p-s. On macOS, you've got Activity Monitor, Force Quit, and Homebrew. Your task: get to a Linux shell, run p-w-d, l-s dash l-a, and d-f dash h, make a file executable with ch-mod, and refresh packages with soo-doo apt update.
